acquisition.why: Inbound through Etsy/Amazon search and Etsy/Meta/Pinterest ads. Agents can draft listings and run ad tests, but creative needs human checks (one source had an AI ad mispronounce the pet's name and present a fake 'review'). This is platform-dependent, and Q4 seasonality makes ad spend risky.

onboarding.why: The customer self-serves with a personalisation form or photo upload. Agents can parse the details and check that the photo is usable.

delivery.why: Physical goods made by a POD partner (Gelato, Printful, InkJoy), so the cap is 0-1. It sits slightly higher because the human-free part is the digital design; any misprint, damage or delay is a physical-world problem. Every personalised design needs a QA gate, e.g. constellation accuracy and AI artefacts [E].

billing.why: The marketplace or Shopify checkout handles payment, and POD supplier costs are charged automatically.

support.why: Personalised items create frequent 'wrong name', 'late' and 'damaged' tickets with no easy resale. Etsy disputes and review management hurt shop standing, so a human is needed for refund calls [E].

scores.R_why: Fits the £300 budget: Shopify or Etsy fees plus a small Etsy Ads test. UK POD partners such as Gelato and Printful EU/UK exist. Constraints: per-order design QA and customer service will eat into 6-8 h/week in Q4, and UK consumer rules apply. Personalised goods are exempt from the 14-day cancellation right, but faulty items are not. Ricardo must also handle UK GDPR for customer photos. Margins on £20-40 items after Etsy fees (~10-15%), ads and shipping are thin [E].
scores.M_why: Extremely saturated: thousands of pet-portrait and star-map sellers with large review counts. One source itself flags AI-generated £10 digital files commoditising Etsy. Image-model access floods themed-photo niches, and Etsy is tightening its AI-art and 'made by' rules. Headroom exists only in sharp micro-niches.
scores.one_line: Low-cost, mostly inbound and partly agent-runnable, but a crowded, AI-commoditised Etsy market with thin margins and physical fulfilment/support exposure makes it a modest test rather than a scalable agent-run business [E].

acquisition.why: Inbound: list on Afternic/Sedo/Dan.com marketplaces with buy-it-now prices, plus a landing page on parked domains. Selling depends on the marketplace.

onboarding.why: The marketplace or escrow handles the buyer process. There is little to onboard.

delivery.why: Agents can scan ExpiredDomains.net or auction lists and score candidates using NameBio comps. Bidding with capital needs human approval. Transfer is handled by escrow or the registrar.

billing.why: Escrow.com or the marketplace handles payment.

support.why: Support is minimal: occasional price negotiation and handling transfer issues.

scores.R_why: The problem is the budget, not the automation. £300 buys only a handful of drop-catch domains plus renewals (~£10-15 each per year). Sell-through rates in the industry are typically around 1-2% a year [E], so a £300 test is statistically unlikely to produce a sale within months. Trademark/UDRP risk needs judgement. The model is legal and doable from the UK.
scores.M_why: A mature market dominated by drop-catch firms and professional portfolios with large capital. AI-driven name valuation is already widespread, and good expired .coms are fiercely contested. Renewal costs keep rising.
scores.one_line: Easy to automate but capital-intensive and illiquid, with professional competitors. The sole source is second-hand with no revenue claims, so it is a poor fit for a £300 agent-run test [E].

acquisition.why: No channel is specified in the sources. Possible routes are SEO or content, Product Hunt, marketplaces or B2B cold email to limited companies. Acquisition is the hardest part and sources say strangers must be convinced to trust an unproven tool; it needs founder judgement [E].

onboarding.why: Self-serve signup is standard for SaaS.

delivery.why: The software runs unattended. Agents can maintain it, but bugs, security and infrastructure need Ricardo's technical review.

billing.why: Stripe subscriptions and Stripe Tax handle billing.

support.why: An AI support bot can handle FAQs, with escalation to Ricardo for bugs.

scores.R_why: Ricardo's technical skills fit, and building costs are low with Claude Code. The binding constraints are distribution and the long runway before revenue at 6-8 h/week, which the sources call 'slowest'. UK GDPR/VAT handling is routine. B2B cold email to limited companies is legal if needed.
scores.M_why: Vibe-coded SaaS has flooded every niche. Generic AI tools are absorbed by frontier models and incumbents. Headroom exists only in narrow, domain-specific workflows.
scores.one_line: Highly automatable once live and suited to a technical founder, but the dossier is vague (no product, customer or revenue). The only first-hand claims are a host's rubric scores, and distribution in a commoditised 2026 market is the unsolved problem [E].

acquisition.why: App Store search (ASO) is organic inbound; agents can do keyword research and metadata iteration, and Apple Search Ads is optional. This is heavily dependent on Apple's ranking algorithm.

onboarding.why: The user installs and hits a paywall or trial, with no human involved.

delivery.why: Unattended software. Single-feature utilities, e.g. sound or text apps, often need little or no backend.

billing.why: Apple IAP/StoreKit (with RevenueCat optional) handles subscriptions, refunds and VAT.

support.why: Apple handles refunds. Support is mostly review replies and occasional emails, which an agent can draft. App review rejections need a human.

scores.R_why: A strong fit for a technical part-timer. The Apple developer account (£79/year) plus a small Search Ads test fits £300. Claude Code builds a v1 in days. Requirements: a Mac/Xcode, UK DSA trader-status disclosure (address and phone published), a privacy policy and UK GDPR compliance. Apple review cycles and the ~60% failure rate mean a portfolio approach is needed.
scores.M_why: Thousands of AI-built clones are now entering low-competition keywords. Apple is increasingly scrutinising aggressive weekly paywalls and clones (guideline 4.3 on spam). ChatGPT substitutes for text utilities. Niche keyword gaps still appear, especially non-AI-substitutable utilities and localisation.
scores.one_line: Probably the best fit: fully inbound, billing and refunds are handled by Apple, the unattended software suits Ricardo's skills, and corroborated first-hand revenue claims ($2.6k-35k MRR) exist. The main risks are Apple policy and keyword saturation [E].

acquisition.why: Legal inbound via short-form video, SEO and paid ads. The proven version needs a human face posting 3-7 reels a day, which an agent cannot do and which conflicts with 6-8 h/week. Faceless AI content plus SEO is the possible agent route, but it is weaker [E].

onboarding.why: Opt-in signup form with double opt-in; PECR-compliant.

delivery.why: Agents can draft and schedule issues on Beehiiv with human editorial approval. Quality and voice determine retention.

billing.why: SparkLoop/Beehiiv ad networks and Stripe for paid tiers are automated. Direct sponsorships need negotiation.

support.why: Minimal support: unsubscribes and the occasional reply.

scores.R_why: The evidence comes from a creator with a viral face-on-camera audience, who is mostly US-focused. Ricardo has no audience, little time, and a toddler, so daily filming is unrealistic. A £300 budget buys only ~100-300 paid UK subscribers at typical £1-3 CPAs [E]. The SparkLoop referral payouts that make paid acquisition viable mainly reward US subscribers.
scores.M_why: Newsletter and creator markets are crowded, AI-generated newsletters are proliferating, and platform algorithms are fickle. Inbox attention is scarce. Niche UK B2B newsletters have some room.
scores.one_line: The model is legal and has good mechanics, but the evidence depends on a human creator's personal brand and high-volume video output, which Ricardo can't supply and agents can't fake well. It works better as a funnel for another business than as a standalone [E].

acquisition.why: Inbound SEO is the primary channel, and agents can do keyword research, content and Search Console iteration. It is highly dependent on Google and AI Overviews. Selling featured listings by DMing sole traders breaches PECR, so monetisation should come from ads, affiliates and inbound paid listings.

onboarding.why: Self-serve listing submission forms; agents moderate.

delivery.why: The site runs itself. Agents can refresh data and fix gaps, with periodic human checks on accuracy and thin content.

billing.why: Ad networks, affiliate programmes and Stripe for featured listings are automated.

support.why: Low volume: listing corrections and takedown requests, which agents can handle with escalation.

scores.R_why: A good fit for Ricardo's technical skills and the £300 budget (domains plus hosting plus tools). Agents can build and iterate it, and time per site is low. SEO takes 6-12 months to compound. UK requirements include cookie consent, UK GDPR for business data, and care with scraped data and listing rights.
scores.M_why: Templated AI directories proliferated during 2024-26, and Google's spam and helpful-content updates plus AI Overviews reduce clicks. Unique proprietary data and UK-specific niches retain some headroom.
scores.one_line: Inbound, cheap, and among the most agent-runnable ideas here, with plausible first-hand revenue ($1-3k/month per portfolio). However, it is a bet on Google traffic surviving AI Overviews and spam updates, and it needs genuinely useful data to avoid being treated as thin content [E].

acquisition.why: Users arrive via inbound SEO. Getting paying providers is the hard part. Under PECR, many UK local tradespeople are sole traders, who cannot be DMed or emailed cold. Cold email to limited companies is OK, and cold calls need TPS/CTPS screening and a human. Otherwise Ricardo must rely on inbound 'claim your listing' flows once traffic exists. The DudeRanch example's first advertisers came from in-person networking at a conference.

onboarding.why: Providers self-serve to claim or upgrade listings via Stripe.

delivery.why: The website and lead routing are automated. Agents refresh listing data, but accuracy needs checks.

support.why: Providers will dispute lead quality and want listing changes. Agents can handle most of this, with escalation to Ricardo.

scores.R_why: Cheap to build and suited to Ricardo's skills. Monetisation requires local SEO traction first, then provider sales. That is slow at 6-8 h/week, and sole-trader-heavy UK trades limit outbound sales. The DudeRanch success relied on an £14k-equivalent premium domain and in-person sales. UK GDPR applies to listing sole traders. Niches with limited-company providers, e.g. house clearance firms, are better.
scores.M_why: Checkatrade, MyBuilder, Bark, Yell and Google Maps/LSAs dominate UK local services. Only narrow niches have room, e.g. specialist suppliers or rural services. AI search may surface providers directly.
scores.one_line: The automatable inbound directory part is fine, but provider monetisation in the UK collides with PECR limits on contacting sole traders and with entrenched incumbents. The single first-hand source is a domain-dependent US outlier, so evidence is weaker than 5 videos suggest [E].

acquisition.why: App Store search and Meta ads are legal inbound channels. The recipe category is broad and expensive to compete in, so success relies on paid social where CAC is often higher than LTV.

delivery.why: LLM API delivery is unattended. Food-safety and allergen outputs need guardrails and periodic review.

support.why: Support is mostly automated, but complaints about bad recipes or allergen issues need human judgement.

scores.R_why: Technically easy for Ricardo, but £300 of Meta ads won't validate a consumer subscription. Allergen and food-safety liability in the UK means careful disclaimers are needed. Per-call LLM costs eat into the low price point.
scores.M_why: Directly substituted by ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, which generate recipes for free. The category is crowded with funded apps (Whisk/Samsung Food, Mealime, SideChef), and Big Tech assistants bundle cooking features.
scores.one_line: A thin LLM wrapper in a category free assistants already serve. The 'first-hand' claims are deal anecdotes, hypotheticals and unfinished launches with no revenue, so this is a poor bet for an agent-run UK business [E].
